entry: Placental [[Mammal|mammal]] in the order Cingulata, native to the Americas. Armadillos form part of the superorder Xenarthra, along with [[Anteater|anteaters]] and [[Sloth|sloths]]. Of the 21 extant species described, some are distinguished by the number of bands on their armor. Living armadillos have a leathery armor shell and long, sharp digging claws. Despite short legs, they can move quite quickly. The average length is about 75 cm (30 in), including the tail; the giant armadillo reaches 150 cm (59 in) and weighs up to 54 kg (119 lb), while the pink fairy armadillo measures only 13–15 cm (5–6 in). When threatened, *Tolypeutes* species roll into a ball, the only armadillos able to do so. Armadillos are classified in two families: Dasypodidae, with *Dasypus* as its only living genus, and Chlamyphoridae, which contains all other living armadillos as well as the glyptodonts. The glyptodonts, up to 1.5 m tall, became extinct around 12,000 years ago.

Landlocked country in the Armenian highlands of West Asia, part of the [[Caucasus]] region. [[Yerevan]] is the capital, largest city and financial center. The Kingdom of Armenia reached its height under [[Tigranes the Great]] in the 1st century BC, and in AD 301 it became the first state to adopt [[Christianity]] as its official religion. The Armenian Apostolic Church remains the primary religious establishment. Eastern Armenia was conquered by the [[Russian Empire]] in the 19th century, and the First Republic of Armenia declared independence in 1918. By 1920 the state had been incorporated into the [[Soviet Union]], and the Republic of Armenia became independent in 1991. Modern Armenia is a unitary, multi-party, democratic nation-state whose economy rests primarily on industrial output and mineral extraction. Armenia supported the Republic of Artsakh ([[Nagorno-Karabakh]]) until [[Azerbaijan]] reincorporated the region through a siege and military offensive in 2023.

Systematic destruction of the Armenian people in the [[Ottoman Empire]] during World War I. The campaign was led by the ruling Committee of Union and Progress and carried out chiefly through the mass murder of around one million Armenians on death marches to the Syrian desert, along with the forced Islamization of others, mainly women and children. Arrests and deportations of Armenian intellectuals and leaders began in Constantinople on 24 April 1915. State-sponsored killings mostly ceased by early 1917, but massacres of survivors continued during the [[Turkish War of Independence]]. The genocide preceded the creation of the Republic of [[Turkey]]. Almost all historians outside Turkey accept it as a historical fact, but the Turkish government maintains that the deportations were legitimate and cannot be described as genocide. Recognition has come from 36 countries.

Indo-European language, the sole member of an independent branch of its family. It is the native language of the Armenian people and the official language of [[Armenia]], and it is spoken widely throughout the diaspora. Estimates of speakers worldwide range from five to seven million. Armenian is written in its own alphabet, introduced in AD 405 by Mesrop Mashtots. The literary history is long, with a 5th-century Bible translation as its oldest surviving text. Its vocabulary was influenced particularly by Parthian, and by Greek, Persian and Syriac. Two standardized literary forms exist: Eastern Armenian, spoken mainly in Armenia, and Western Armenian, originally spoken in present-day [[Turkey]] and, since the [[Armenian genocide]], mostly in the diaspora. The two are mutually intelligible after significant exposure. Armenians are mentioned in the 6th-century BC Behistun Inscription and in [[Xenophon]]'s 4th-century BC history, the *Anabasis*.

Theological tradition within [[Protestantism]] based on the ideas of Dutch Reformed theologian [[Jacobus Arminius]]. It emerged in the early 17th century as a structured response to Calvinist predestination. Arminius's followers, known as the Remonstrants, drafted the Five Articles of Remonstrance in 1610. Central to the tradition is the belief that God extends prevenient grace to all people, preparing them for regeneration, and that the grace enabling regeneration and sanctification can be resisted. At the Synod of Dort, which was open primarily to Dutch Calvinists, the Arminians were excluded, and in 1618 the synod condemned Arminius and his followers as heretics. The two main variants are Classical Arminianism, associated with Arminius, and Wesleyan Arminianism, associated with [[John Wesley]]. [[Baptists]] in the 17th century, [[Methodism|Methodists]] in the 18th century and Pentecostals in the 20th century were influenced by Arminian views.

Germanic chieftain of the Cherusci tribe. He commanded an alliance of Germanic tribes at the [[Battle of the Teutoburg Forest]] in AD 9, in which three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus were destroyed. The victory precipitated the [[Roman Empire]]'s permanent strategic withdrawal from Germania Magna, and modern historians regard it as one of Imperial Rome's greatest defeats. Born a prince, he learned Latin and served in the Roman military, gaining Roman citizenship, before secretly plotting the revolt. He later fought retaliatory invasions by the Roman general Germanicus. He sought to become king and was assassinated by rivals. [[Tacitus]] described him as the liberator of the Germanic tribes. In the 19th century German nationalists hailed him as a symbol of German unity and freedom.

Annual commemoration, held on 11 November, of the armistice that halted fighting in [[World War I]]. The armistice was signed by the Allies and Germany at Compiègne, France, and took effect at 11:00 a.m. on 11 November 1918. It initially ran for 36 days and was extended several times, and a formal peace was reached only with the [[Treaty of Versailles]] the following year. The day is a national holiday in France and in many Allied countries, several of which later renamed it [[Remembrance Day]] in the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] or Veterans Day in the [[United States]].

Use of armored fighting vehicles, chiefly tanks, in war. Armored warfare relies on the penetration of defensive lines by maneuvering armored units, supported by [[Infantry|infantry]] fighting vehicles, self-propelled [[Artillery]] and other combat vehicles. Its doctrine was developed to break the static trench warfare of [[World War I]] on the Western Front. Britain and France first developed tanks in 1915, and British Mark I tanks first went into action at the Somme in 1916 without breaking the deadlock. British tanks were more successful at Cambrai in 1917, where they broke the Hindenburg Line. Germany produced 20 A7V tanks during the war, compared with over 4,400 French and over 2,500 British tanks. The first tank-versus-tank battle took place at Villers-Bretonneux in April 1918. In [[World War II]], large armored operations, such as the 1940 Western Campaign, enabled swift territorial conquests.

Armed force that fights primarily on land, the land-based branch of a nation's military. Armies are divided into specialties according to mission, role and training. Common groupings include [[Infantry]], armored corps, [[Artillery]], signal corps, special forces, military police and medical corps. In some countries, such as France and China, the term refers more broadly to the armed forces as a whole. Regular armies use standardized doctrines, uniforms and organizations. [[Ancient Egypt]] established one of the first professional standing armies, which in the Middle and New Kingdoms became a permanent force with specialized divisions, standardized weaponry and war chariots. During the Iron Age the Maurya and Nanda Empires of India had one of the largest armies in the world, peaking at over 600,000 infantry.

Austrian and American modernist composer, music theorist and teacher. He taught in [[Vienna]] and at the Prussian Academy of Arts from 1925 to 1933, resigning in anticipation of Nazi Germany's civil-service restrictions. He reaffirmed his Judaism before immigrating to the United States, where he taught at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] from 1936 to 1944. Schoenberg mentored Anton Webern and Alban Berg, and with them he was associated with the Second Viennese School, which began writing atonal, expressionist music. He arrived at twelve-tone technique by 1923, and used it in works such as the Variations for Orchestra (1926–1928). His innovative music shaped at least three generations of composers, including Milton Babbitt and [[Pierre Boulez]], and his views influenced [[Theodor W. Adorno]].

Austrian-American actor, former professional bodybuilder and politician. He won the Mr. Universe title at age 20 and the [[Mr. Olympia]] title seven times. After retiring from bodybuilding he became a Hollywood action star, starring in *Conan the Barbarian* (1982) and as the Terminator in the *Terminator* franchise. His other action films include *Predator* (1987), *Total Recall* (1990) and *True Lies* (1994). As a registered member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he chaired the President's Council on Physical Fitness and Sports during most of the [[George H. W. Bush]] administration. He served as the 38th governor of [[California]] from 2003 to 2011, after winning a special recall election. He later returned to acting, starring in the *Expendables* films.

[[Oil painting]] on oak panel by [[Jan van Eyck]], dated 1434 and held by the [[National Gallery]], London. It is believed to depict the Italian merchant Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini and his wife, probably in their residence at [[Bruges]], [[Flanders]]. It is considered one of the most original and complex paintings in Western art, combining geometric perspective with a mirror that expands the picture space. Van Eyck applied thin translucent glazes and painted wet-in-wet, producing an intensity of tone and color and a convincing depiction of textures and light. Erwin Panofsky considered it a unique form of marriage contract recorded as a painting, while Craig Harbison argued that it is tempting to call it the first genre painting of modern times. The painting was bought by the National Gallery in 1842.

[[Organic compound|Organic]] compound, or arene, with a chemistry typified by [[Benzene]]. Aromatic compounds are cyclic compounds satisfying Hückel's rule. The term no longer relates to odor, although the grouping originally arose from the smells of early-discovered molecules. They are typically unreactive, often nonpolar and hydrophobic, and burn with a strong sooty yellow flame. In heteroarenes, an atom such as [[Oxygen]], [[Nitrogen]] or [[Sulfur]] replaces a carbon in the ring. Benzene, C₆H₆, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon; its six electrons are shared equally in delocalized pi [[Molecular orbital|molecular orbitals]] around the ring. Industrially important aromatic hydrocarbons include benzene, [[Toluene]] and xylene, collectively called BTX.

Form of long gun that appeared in Europe and the [[Ottoman Empire]] in the 15th century. The name derives from the Dutch *haakbus*, or hook gun, after the hook on early models that steadied them against battlements. The addition of a shoulder stock and a matchlock mechanism in the late 15th century made it a handheld [[Firearm|firearm]] and the first with a trigger. A heavier version, then called a [[Musket]], was developed around 1521 to better penetrate plate armor. The matchlock arquebus is considered the forerunner of the flintlock musket.

Marriage in which the spouses are selected by a third party, most commonly their parents. Couples normally agree to the arrangement, unlike a forced marriage, in which a partner does not consent, or a child marriage, in which a partner is under 18. The [[United Nations]] condemns marriages without consent. Arranged marriages were the norm throughout the world until the 18th century and remain widespread in [[South Asia]], West Asia, North Africa, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. They declined substantially in [[Europe]] and East Asia after the 19th century. In the [[United States]] they were common among migrant families until the first half of the 20th century. In [[China]] they were the norm before the mid-20th century.

Formula for the temperature dependence of chemical reaction rates. [[Svante Arrhenius]] proposed it in 1889 at Leipzig University, building on the work of [[Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff|van 't Hoff]]. The rate constant is given by k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT), where Eₐ is the molar activation energy. The temperature dependence arises because a greater fraction of molecular collisions have enough energy to exceed the activation barrier as temperature rises. The equation is best seen as an empirical relationship.

Group of medical conditions characterized by irregular heartbeat. Arrhythmias are deviations from the normal sinus rhythm. A resting heart rate above 100 beats per minute in adults is called [[Tachycardia]], and one below 60 is called bradycardia. Some arrhythmias cause no symptoms, while others cause palpitations, lightheadedness, fainting or chest pain. Some predispose a person to [[Stroke]] or [[Heart failure]], and others may result in sudden death. Treatments include medications, pacemakers and urgent cardioversion or defibrillation.

[[Starch]] obtained from the rhizomes of several tropical plants, traditionally *Maranta arundinacea*. Tapioca from [[Cassava]] is often also labeled arrowroot. Archaeological studies in the [[Americas]] show cultivation as early as 7,000 years ago. The name may derive from *aru-aru*, meaning "meal of meals" in the language of the Caribbean Arawak people, for whom the plant was a staple. The starch was once widely used in carbonless copy paper because of its grain size. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines' arrowroot industry contributed close to 50% of the country's foreign export earnings from the 1930s to the 1960s. In 1998/99 the industry produced 312,000 lb (142,000 kg) of starch, about 3% of the peak level of the 1960s.

Fictional gentleman thief and master of disguise created in 1905 by French writer Maurice Leblanc. The character debuted in short stories in the magazine *Je sais tout*, beginning with "The Arrest of Arsène Lupin" on July 15, 1905. Lupin is often described as the criminal counterpart to [[Sherlock Holmes]]. After legal objections from [[Arthur Conan Doyle]], Holmes was renamed "Herlock Sholmès" in Leblanc's stories. Leblanc wrote 17 novels and 39 novellas featuring Lupin.

French football manager, nicknamed *Le Professeur*, who led [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] from 1996 to 2018. He was the club's longest-serving and most successful manager and the first foreign manager to win a Premier League and FA Cup double, in 1998. He led Arsenal to an unbeaten league title in 2004 and to the [[UEFA Champions League]] final in 2006. Wenger has been [[FIFA]]'s chief of global football development since 2019.

Professional association football club based in Islington, North London, competing in the [[Premier League]]. Founded in 1886 as Dial Square by workers at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, the club moved to Highbury in 1913 and to the Emirates Stadium in 2006. Arsenal has won 14 league titles, a record 14 FA Cups and two League Cups. It reached the [[UEFA Champions League]] final in 2006. Under [[Arsène Wenger]] the club won three league titles and seven FA Cups, including the unbeaten 2003–04 season.

Chemical element with the symbol As and atomic number 33, classified as a [[Metalloid|metalloid]]. Arsenic is notoriously toxic. It occurs naturally in many minerals, usually combined with [[Sulfur]] and metals, and its grey allotrope is the only form important to industry. Its primary use is in alloys of [[Lead]], as in car batteries and ammunition. Arsenic is also an n-type dopant in semiconductors and a component of gallium arsenide. Its compounds, especially the trioxide, were used in pesticides, treated wood and herbicides, though these uses are declining. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency states that all forms of arsenic are a serious risk to human health, and it is classified as a Group 1 [[Carcinogen]]. Arsenic contamination of [[Groundwater]] affects millions of people worldwide.

Style of visual arts, architecture and product design that first appeared in Paris in the 1910s and flourished internationally in the 1920s and early 1930s. The name, short for *arts décoratifs*, comes from the 1925 Exposition internationale des arts décoratifs et industriels modernes in Paris. Art Deco drew on the bold geometric forms of [[Cubism]] and the Vienna Secession, and on styles from ancient Egypt, China and Japan. It used luxury materials such as ebony and ivory, and new materials such as chrome, [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] and plastic. The [[Empire State Building]] in New York is a monument to the style, and [[Miami|Miami Beach]] has the largest concentration of Art Deco architecture in the world. During the [[Great Depression]] a sleeker Streamline Moderne appeared. After the outbreak of [[World War II]], the style lost its dominance to the functional styles of modern architecture.

International style of art, architecture and applied art, popular between 1890 and 1910. It was often inspired by natural forms such as the curves of plants and flowers, using asymmetry and whiplash lines and modern materials such as iron, glass and ceramics. It aimed to break down the distinction between fine arts and applied arts, and it reacted against the historicism of 19th-century architecture. The first Art Nouveau houses appeared in [[Brussels]] in the 1890s, notably those of Victor Horta, whose Hôtel Tassel was completed in 1893. The style peaked at the 1900 [[Paris]] International Exposition and in the Paris Métro entrances designed by Hector Guimard. In Germany it was known as *Jugendstil*, and in Italy as *Stile Liberty*. By 1914 it was largely exhausted, and in the 1920s it was replaced by [[Art Deco]] and then modernism.

Discussion or evaluation of visual art, usually in the context of aesthetics. Art criticism divides into historical criticism, a form of art history, and contemporary criticism of work by living artists. Some movements were named disparagingly by critics before artists adopted the names, as with [[Impressionism]] and [[Cubism]]. Critics of the past are often ridiculed for dismissing artists now venerated, such as the early Impressionists. Early forms of criticism appear in the works of [[Plato]], [[Vitruvius]] and [[Augustine of Hippo]]. From the Renaissance, wealthy patrons employed intermediary art-evaluators. [[Denis Diderot]] pioneered salon reviews in the 18th and 19th centuries. Methods range from recording immediate impressions to systematic analysis using technical knowledge, aesthetic theory and sociocultural context.
